'''William Morgan Jackson''' (born September 24, 1936) is a Distinguished Research and [[Emeritus Professor]] of Chemistry at [[University of California, Davis]] and pioneer in the field of [[astrochemistry]]. His work considers cometary astrochemistry and the development of [[laser]] [[photochemistry]] to understand planetary atmospheres. He is a Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], the [[American Physical Society]] and the [[American Chemical Society]]. In addition to contributing research work, he is notable as a mentor and advocate for increasing minority participation in science, and was one of the founders of the [[National Organization for the Professional Advancement of Black Chemists and Chemical Engineers]] (NOBCChE).<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jones |first=Dave |date=2021-04-27 |title=National Science Board Honors Chemistry Professor William Jackson for Public Service |url=https://www.ucdavis.edu/news/national-science-board-honors-chemistry-professor-william-jackson-public-service |access-date=2022-04-10 |website=UC Davis |language=en}}</ref>

In 2019, he was awarded the [[Astronomical Society of the Pacific]] Arthur B.C. Walker II Award for his research and commitment to promoting diversity.<ref name=":8">{{Cite web|title=Astronomical Society of the Pacific : WHO WE ARE : Awards : Arthur B.C. Walker II Award|url=https://astrosociety.org/who-we-are/awards/arthur-bc-walker-ii-award.html|access-date=2020-10-05|website=astrosociety.org|language=en}}</ref> In 2021, he was awarded the [[American Physical Society]] Julius Edgar [[Lilienfeld Prize]] for outstanding contributions to fundamental [[chemical physics]] and [[spectroscopy]] associated with asteroids and comets, and for exemplary teaching at both the undergraduate and graduate levels, as well as lifelong service and inspiration to a diverse community.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web|title=Julius Edgar Lilienfeld Prize|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/lilienfeld.cfm|access-date=2020-10-05|website=www.aps.org|language=en}}</ref>

== Early life ==
Jackson was born in [[Birmingham, Alabama]] to William Morgan and Claudia H. Jackson on September 24, 1936.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jackson |first1=William M. |title=A Black Scientist's Retrospective of His Life in Physical Chemistry |journal=[[The Journal of Physical Chemistry A]] |date=8 July 2021 |volume=125 |issue=26 |pages=5711–5717 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpca.1c05194 |pmid=34259000 |bibcode=2021JPCA..125.5711J |issn=1089-5639|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-ydHVdMUqdEC&pg=PA181|title=Distinguished African American Scientists of the 20th Century|last1=Kessler|first1=James H.|last2=Morin|first2=Katherine A.|last3=Kidd|first3=J. S.|last4=Kidd|first4=Renee A.|date=1996|publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group|isbn=9780897749558|language=en}}</ref> He grew up in a segregated society and spent part of his childhood in Dynamite Hill, an area in [[Birmingham, Alabama|Birmingham]] that the [[Ku Klux Klan]] frequently bombed during the [[Civil rights movement]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://lettersandscience.ucdavis.edu/blog/william-jackson-honored-research-and-mentoring|title=William Jackson Honored for Research and Mentoring|last=Oskin|first=Becky|website=lettersandscience.ucdavis.edu|date=24 July 2019 |language=en|access-date=2019-09-05}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last1=Elliott |first1=Debbie |url=https://www.npr.org/sections/codeswitch/2013/07/06/197342590/remembering-birminghams-dynamite-hill-neighborhood|title=Remembering Birmingham's 'Dynamite Hill' Neighborhood|website=NPR.org|date=6 July 2013 |language=en|access-date=2019-09-05}}</ref> His father, a [[Tuskegee University]] graduate, owned the Apex Cab Company and also taught auto mechanics at [[Parker High School (Alabama)|Parker High School]], whilst his mother, a graduate of [[Santa Barbara City College|Santa Barbara Junior College]], worked for the [[Federal government of the United States|US government]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jackson |first=William M. |date=2019-03-14 |title=Autobiography of "William M. Jackson, Jr." |journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A |volume=123 |issue=10 |pages=1908–1913 |doi=10.1021/acs.jpca.8b12310 |pmid=30866631 |bibcode=2019JPCA..123.1908J |issn=1089-5639|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name=":0" /> At the age of nine, Jackson contracted [[polio]] and had to spend a year out of school.<ref name=":0" />

== Education ==
After completing tenth grade, Jackson joined [[Morehouse College]] as an early entrance student.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Auburn University |url=http://www.auburn.edu/ |access-date=2019-09-05 |website=Auburn University |language=en}}</ref> He was awarded a full scholarship.<ref name=":2" /> At first Jackson considered majoring in [[mathematics]], but decided to study chemistry after meeting [[Henry Cecil McBay]].<ref name=":0" /> He graduated in 1956 and applied to several graduate schools, including [[Northwestern University]] and [[Purdue University]]. He received a response from [[Northwestern University|Northwestern]], who said that they had already fulfilled their three fellowships for [[African Americans|African American]] students.<ref name=":0" /> Eventually he moved [[Washington, D.C.]], where he got a job and lived with his cousin.<ref name=":0" /> He studied at the [[Catholic University of America]], where he was awarded a postgraduate research fellowship.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.scienceupdate.com/spotlights/african-american-scientists/|title=Science Update: The Science Radio News Feature of the AAAS|access-date=2019-09-05}}</ref> During his doctoral studies, he worked in the [[Harry Diamond Laboratories]], where he studied [[molten salt]] compounds.<ref name=":0" /> During the final year of his PhD, Jackson's wife became pregnant, and Jackson took time out of graduate school to earn money.<ref name=":0" /> During this time he worked at the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]].<ref name=":0" /> He returned to the [[Catholic University of America]] where he studied gasoline additives.<ref name=":0" /> After earning his PhD in 1961, he joined the [[Lockheed Martin]], where he worked on [[formaldehyde]] resins and ways to protect missiles as they reenter the [[Atmosphere of Earth]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=https://chemistry.ucdavis.edu/people/william-jackson|title=William Jackson {{!}} Chemistry|website=chemistry.ucdavis.edu|date=12 September 2017 |language=en|access-date=2019-09-05}}</ref> He returned to the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] as a postdoctoral researcher, studying how [[radiant energy]] impacted chemical structures.<ref name=":0" /> He investigated how radiation impacted the coating applied to space vehicles.<ref name=":0" />

== Research and careers ==
In 1964, Jackson joined the [[Goddard Space Flight Center]].<ref name=":2" /> It was here that he became interested in the origins of [[free radicals]] in comets.<ref name=":2" /> <!-- American English edit -->While at the [[Goddard Space Flight Center]] he proposed to use the [[International Ultraviolet Explorer]] satellite to look for comets.<ref name=":2" /> Using the [[Haystack Observatory]], Jackson made measurements of water emission in comets.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Goodson|first1=Theodore|last2=Houston|first2=Paul L.|last3=McCrary|first3=Victor R. |authorlink3=Victor McCrary |date=2019-03-14|title=A Tribute to William M. Jackson, Jr.|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A|volume=123|issue=10|pages=1905–1907|doi=10.1021/acs.jpca.8b12308|pmid=30866632|bibcode=2019JPCA..123.1905G |s2cid=76664629|issn=1089-5639}}</ref> He joined the faculty at the [[University of Pittsburgh]] in 1969, where he spent a year researching and teaching.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.indianapolisrecorder.com/article_3f9f0385-c51c-5a77-a088-dba99087a632.html|title=INVENTORS & INVENTIONS|website=Indianapolis Recorder Newspaper|language=en|access-date=2019-09-05}}</ref> At the [[University of Pittsburgh]], he worked with Wade Fite and Ted Brackman on the detection of electron impact on molecules using [[mass spectrometry]].<ref name=":4" /> A year later he returned to [[Goddard Space Flight Center|Goddard]], where he developed a system to detect [[free radicals]] using laser beams.<ref name=":0" />

In 1974, one of Jackson's colleagues, a professor of chemistry at [[Howard University]], died suddenly.<ref name=":0" /> Jackson agreed to teach his course for the rest of the term and was subsequently appointed to a joint position in chemistry and physics.<ref name=":0" /> Here he began working on [[laser-induced fluorescence]] (LIF) to study the [[rovibronic coupling]] in cyano radicals.<ref name=":4" /> He was the first person to demonstrate LIF could be used to study molecular photodissociation.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Jackson|first=William M.|date=1973-07-15|title=Laser induced fluorescence of CN radicals|journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics|volume=59|issue=2|pages=960–961|doi=10.1063/1.1680120|bibcode=1973JChPh..59..960J |issn=0021-9606}}</ref> He primarily studied comets using satellites ground-based telescopes, using experimental data and theoretical predictions to establish how the [[free radicals]] inside comets form. Despite having left [[Goddard Space Flight Center]], Jackson served as team leader for the [[International Ultraviolet Explorer]] telescope, which observed [[Halley's Comet]].<ref name=":2" /> He joined [[University of California, Davis]] in 1985 and was promoted to Distinguished Professor in 1998.<ref name=":1" /> The Jackson laboratory ("Jackson's Photon Crusaders") developed [[tunable laser]]s that could be used to detect and characterize [[free radicals]].<ref name=":4" /> These included [[excimer laser]]s, nitrogen-pumped lasers and an Alexandrite laser.<ref name=":4" /> By building laser systems in the laboratory, Jackson helped to establish the excited states of molecules that are present in planetary atmospheres. The experiments consisted of one laser for the [[photodissociation]] of the parent molecule, and another laser to excite the [[free radical]] into an excited state. When the excited molecule fluoresced back to the ground state, the fluorescence was captured in a [[photomultiplier tube]].<ref name=":4" /> He has investigated the photochemistry of [[carbon monoxide]], [[nitrogen]] and [[carbon dioxide]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last1=Goodson|first1=Theodore|last2=Houston|first2=Paul L.|last3=McCrary|first3=Victor R.|date=2019-03-14|title=A Tribute to William M. Jackson, Jr.|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A|volume=123|issue=10|pages=1905–1907|doi=10.1021/acs.jpca.8b12308|pmid=30866632|bibcode=2019JPCA..123.1905G |s2cid=76664629|issn=1089-5639}}</ref> His laser systems exploit resonant [[four-wave mixing]], which allows them to [[Photodissociation|photodissociate]] gases observed in planetary atmospheres.<ref name=":5" /> He also showed that it is possible to ionise the resulting atomic fragments using a velocity imaging [[Time-of-flight mass spectrometry|time-of-flight mass spectrometer]].<ref name=":5" />

In 1996 [[The Planetary Society]] named asteroid 1081 EE37 as (4322) ''Billjackson'' in his honour.<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|url=https://www.thehistorymakers.org/biography/william-jackson|title=William Jackson's Biography|website=The HistoryMakers|language=en|access-date=2019-09-05}}</ref> He served as Chair of the Department of Chemistry at [[University of California, Davis]] in 2000.<ref name=":6" /> He retired in 2006, but has continued to research and recruit students.<ref name=":2" /> In 2013, he was made the Emile A. Dickenson Professor at [[University of California, Davis]].<ref name=":3" /> In 2019 the [[The Journal of Physical Chemistry A|Journal of Physical Chemistry]] dedicated a special issue to Jackson.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://pubs.acs.org/toc/jpcafh/123/10|title=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A {{!}} Vol 123, No 10|website=pubs.acs.org|language=en|access-date=2019-09-05}}</ref>

== Academic service and advocacy ==
Jackson has campaigned for equity, diversity and inclusion in science since he started his career.<ref name=":1" /> He was one of the founders of the [[National Organization for the Professional Advancement of Black Chemists and Chemical Engineers]] (NOBCChE).<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":6" /> The organization began to promote and award minority scientists and engineers, as well as encouraging high school students to consider studying science or engineering. It was supported by [[Ted Kennedy]] and the [[National Science Foundation]].<ref name=":2" /> Jackson served as NOBCChE's first treasurer from 1973.<ref name=":7"/> He stated that he was inspired to start the NOBCChE after attending a meeting of the [[American Chemical Society]], and seeing no African Americans there.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|url=http://cen-cc-origin.acs.org/articles/91/i44/Paying-Forward-NOBCChE.html|title=Paying It Forward At NOBCChE {{!}} November 4, 2013 Issue - Vol. 91 Issue 44 {{!}} Chemical & Engineering News|website=cen-cc-origin.acs.org|access-date=2019-09-05}}</ref> He has served in various capacities for the NOBCChE, attending every annual meeting other than one ([[San Diego]], 1999) in protest of the [[1996 California Proposition 209]].<ref name=":7" /> He provided evidence to Congress in an effort to increase research funding to [[historically black colleges and universities]].<ref name=":1" /> When he arrived at U.C. Davis, only two students from underrepresented minorities had ever earned chemistry PhDs there. While at UC Davis, he secured funding from the [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]] and increased the department's minority student population to about 15% of the academic cohort.<ref name=":2" /> Jackson was known for bringing students and researchers to his laboratory "who were the stones the builders rejected, and he made them the cornerstones for future scientific research".<ref name=":4" />

* 2004 Elected Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]<ref name=":3" />

Jackson Jr.|date=2019-07-30|website=UC Davis|language=EN|access-date=2019-09-05}}</ref>
